name: Christoph Ingenhoven
bio:
Christoph Ingenhoven (born 1960) is a German architect based in Düsseldorf, known for buildings designed around daylight, natural ventilation and low energy use, an approach he calls "supergreen". Born in Düsseldorf, he studied at RWTH Aachen and, for a year, with Hans Hollein at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf, and founded his office in the city in 1985. He drew wide notice in 1991, when his team shared the jury prize with Norman Foster in the competition for the Commerzbank Tower in Frankfurt, and international recognition with the RWE Tower in Essen (1997), one of the world's first ecological high-rise buildings. He received the European Prize for Architecture in 2022.

His completed works include the European Investment Bank in Luxembourg (2008). 1 Bligh Street in Sydney (2011), designed with Architectus, is a 30-storey office tower with Australia's first full double-skin façade on a major high-rise, external louvres that turn with the sun and a naturally ventilated atrium 120 metres high; it won the International High-Rise Award. The Lanserhof Sylt (2022) won both MIPIM and WAF awards in 2023.

name: Diller Scofidio + Renfro
bio:
Diller Scofidio + Renfro is a New York design studio that works across architecture, the visual arts and the performing arts. It was founded in 1981 by the architects Elizabeth Diller and Ricardo Scofidio; Charles Renfro joined in 1997 and became a partner in 2004, and Benjamin Gilmartin became the fourth partner in 2015. In 1999 it was the first architecture firm to receive a MacArthur Fellowship, the foundation saying it had "created an alternative form of architectural practice that unites design, performance, and electronic media with cultural and architectural theory and criticism".

The Institute of Contemporary Art, Boston (2006) was one of the studio's first buildings and the first new art museum in Boston in over a century. The High Line in New York (2009), designed with James Corner Field Operations and Piet Oudolf, turned a disused 1.45-mile railway spur on Manhattan's West Side into an elevated park that opened in phases from 2009 to 2014. Zaryadye Park in Moscow (2017), beside Red Square, came from a 2012 competition its team won against 90 entries, with terraces planted as forest, steppe, tundra and floodplain.

name: DP Architects
bio:
DP Architects is a Singapore architecture practice, founded in 1967 as Design Partnership by William Lim Siew Wai, Tay Kheng Soon and Koh Seow Chuan. It is best known at home for People's Park Complex and Golden Mile Complex, from the late 1960s and early 1970s; on a visit in 2005 Rem Koolhaas said of them, "These buildings were not intended to be landmarks, but became landmarks." Re-formed as DP Architects in 1975, the group now counts among the largest practices in the world, with 18 offices and more than 900 staff.

Esplanade - Theatres on the Bay (2002), designed with Michael Wilford & Partners until that firm left the project in 1995, is two rounded space frames fitted with triangulated glass and sunshades, and is nicknamed "The Durian". The Singapore Flyer (2008), with Kisho Kurokawa's office, is a 165-metre observation wheel that was the tallest in the world when completed. The National Stadium, Singapore (2014), with Arup and AECOM, is covered by an 83-metre-high steel dome with a retractable roof and is naturally ventilated.

name: Edwin Lutyens
bio:
Sir Edwin Lutyens (1869–1944) was a British architect known for adapting traditional styles to the needs of his time, in English country houses, war memorials and public buildings. He set up his own practice in 1888. His partnership with the garden designer Gertrude Jekyll, which began with her house at Munstead Wood, shaped many of his country houses. After the First World War he designed the Cenotaph in Whitehall and the Memorial to the Missing of the Somme at Thiepval. He received the RIBA Royal Gold Medal in 1921.

He had an instrumental role in building New Delhi, part of which is still called "Lutyens' Delhi". For the Viceroy's House, now Rashtrapati Bhavan (1929), begun in 1912, he invented his own classical order, the Delhi Order, and set the dome on a drum whose decoration recalls the railings around early Buddhist stupas such as Sanchi. For Sansad Bhavan (Old Parliament House) (1927), designed with Herbert Baker, he proposed the circular plan, which he thought most efficient for its triangular site. Farther afield he designed the Johannesburg Art Gallery (1915), with 15 exhibition halls and sculpture gardens.

name: Egon Eiermann
bio:
Egon Eiermann (1904–1970) was a German architect and furniture designer, one of the most prominent German architects of the second half of the 20th century. Born near Potsdam, he studied at the Technical University of Berlin and was a master student of Hans Poelzig from 1925 to 1928. He practised in Berlin from 1931, and after the war moved to Karlsruhe, where he taught from 1947 and worked on steel-frame construction; his transparent steel-frame factories of the rebuilding years became models. With Sep Ruf he designed West Germany's pavilion at the 1958 Brussels World's Fair.

The Matthäuskirche Pforzheim (1953) preceded his best-known work, the Kaiser Wilhelm Memorial Church in Berlin (1963). He won its 1956 competition proposing to clear the bomb-damaged ruin, but public outcry led him to keep the remnant of the old spire between a new octagonal church and a hexagonal tower. The church walls are a concrete honeycomb holding 21,292 pieces of stained glass by Gabriel Loire. The Langer Eugen in Bonn (1969), commissioned in 1965, held the offices of the members of the Bundestag until parliament moved to Berlin in 1999.

name: Francisco Ramos de Azevedo
bio:
Francisco de Paula Ramos de Azevedo (1851–1928) was a Brazilian architect known for designing many of São Paulo's landmarks, among them the Pinacoteca (1893). Born in São Paulo to a wealthy family from Campinas, he went to Ghent in Belgium in 1878 to study civil engineering but graduated in architecture in 1886, trained in classical design but drawn to eclecticism. Back in Brazil he began in Campinas, where he completed the cathedral, then designed houses for São Paulo's elite. He was a founder and director of the Polytechnic School, now part of the University of São Paulo, and directed the Liceu de Artes e Ofícios.

The Theatro Municipal de São Paulo (1911), built from 1903 with the Italian architects Cláudio and Domiziano Rossi, opened on 12 September 1911. His office was hired in 1911 for the Palace of Justice of São Paulo (1933), modelled on the Palace of Justice in Rome; he supervised the work until his death, and Ricardo Severo and Arnaldo Dumont Villares finished it. The Municipal Market of São Paulo (1933) was likewise inaugurated after he died.

name: Friedrich Silaban
bio:
Friedrich Silaban (1912–1984) was an Indonesian architect whose best-known designs were commissioned under President Sukarno, and who preferred modernism to traditional Indonesian styles. Born in Bonan Dolok, now in Samosir Regency, the son of a Batak Protestant pastor, he studied building at the Koningin Wilhelmina School in Batavia and in Pontianak designed the Equator Monument (1938). He studied at the Academy of Architecture in Amsterdam in 1949–50, and in 1959 co-founded the Indonesian Institute of Architects. He left out traditional ornament, arguing that an Indonesian architecture did not need to imitate traditional forms.

He won the design competition for the Istiqlal Mosque in Jakarta (1978), according to his son under a pseudonym because he was a Protestant; the national mosque opened in 1978. For the Gelora Bung Karno Stadium (1962), built for the Asian Games that year, he persuaded Sukarno to place the sports complex at Senayan rather than Dukuh Atas to avoid future traffic; it opened with 110,000 seats. His 1955 entry for the National Monument (Indonesia) (1975) was ranked highest by the jury yet placed second, and the monument was finally designed by Soedarsono.

name: Future Systems
bio:
Future Systems was a London architecture and design practice founded in 1979 by the Czech architect Jan Kaplický and David Nixon. Through the 1980s it was known mainly for experimental, largely unbuilt designs drawing on aerospace and car engineering and on forms found in nature, above all the curved monocoque shells of aircraft, cars and boats. Amanda Levete became a partner in 1989, and the practice moved towards built work, starting with the Hauer-King House in Islington (1994). Kaplický and Levete divided the firm in 2008; Kaplický kept the name and died in Prague in January 2009, after which Future Systems ceased.

The Lord's Media Centre in London (1999) has an aluminium semi-monocoque body made with boat- and aircraft-building methods; it won the 1999 Stirling Prize. The Selfridges Building, Birmingham (2003) wraps a street corner in a curved façade of 15,000 anodised aluminium discs on a blue ground, an example of what became known as blobitecture. The Museo Enzo Ferrari in Modena (2012) adds a 6,000-square-metre gallery of Ferrari cars beside the house and workshop of Enzo Ferrari's father.

name: Gigon/Guyer
bio:
Gigon/Guyer, or Annette Gigon / Mike Guyer Architects, is a Zurich architecture office led by Annette Gigon, born in Herisau in 1959, and Mike Guyer, born in Columbus, Ohio, in 1958. Both graduated from ETH Zurich in 1984; Gigon then worked for Herzog & de Meuron and Guyer for OMA in Rotterdam, and they set up the joint office in 1989. It wins most of its commissions as first prize in competitions, and since 2012 the two have held a joint professorship at ETH Zurich. The office is admired for its handling of materials and colour. Since 2000 its work has spread from houses and museums to housing and offices.

The practice made its name in the 1990s with museums whose interiors are typically simple, white-painted rooms within a subdued, material-based palette. The Kirchner Museum Davos (1992), designed from 1989 and devoted to the art of Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, was followed by the Museum Liner (Kunstmuseum Appenzell) (1998). In Zürich the Prime Tower (2011), a 126-metre office tower, was the tallest building in Switzerland until the Roche Tower in Basel overtook it in 2015.

name: Giles Gilbert Scott
bio:
Sir Giles Gilbert Scott (1880–1960) was a British architect noted for blending the Gothic tradition with modernism, and the designer of the red telephone box. Born in Hampstead, London, into a family of architects, he was the grandson of Sir George Gilbert Scott, designer of the Albert Memorial, and became an articled pupil of Temple Moore in 1899. His industrial buildings include Battersea Power Station and Bankside Power Station, now Tate Modern. He was president of the RIBA in 1933 and received its Royal Gold Medal in 1925.

In 1903, aged 22 and with no buildings to his name, he was chosen as architect of Liverpool Cathedral (1978); the Lady Chapel was consecrated in 1910, and the cathedral was finished nearly two decades after his death. Cambridge University Library (1934), built from 1931, has a 157-foot tower that John D. Rockefeller persuaded him to add for a grander entrance. For the New Bodleian Library in Oxford, now the Weston Library (1940), he had to store millions of books without rising above the neighbouring buildings, so he built deep into the ground behind two low façades.

name: Giovanni Michelucci
bio:
Giovanni Michelucci (1891–1990) was an Italian architect, urban planner and designer. Born in Pistoia into a family that ran an iron workshop, he graduated from Florence's Higher Institute of Architecture in 1911 and became dean of the Florence architecture faculty in 1944, moving to the engineering faculty in Bologna in 1948. Much of his later work, from housing and churches to prisons and hospitals, grew from his idea of an open, democratic "New City", and in 1982 he set up a foundation for research on the city.

As coordinator of the Gruppo Toscano he won the 1933 competition for Firenze Santa Maria Novella Station (1935), acclaimed internationally for its rational, functional design and for how it fits its historic setting. The Church of the Autostrada del Sole (1964) at Campi Bisenzio, built to honour the workers who died building the motorway, sets a cross plan and stone walls under a tent-like copper roof. After the Vajont Dam disaster of 1963 destroyed Longarone, he designed the town's new church, Santa Maria Immacolata, Longarone (1983), on the site of the old one.

name: Günther Domenig
bio:
Günther Domenig (1934–2012) was an Austrian architect from Klagenfurt whose work moved from brutalism through pop architecture to an expressive, counter-modernist style. He studied at the Graz University of Technology and from 1963 to 1973 practised with Eilfried Huth; their exposed-concrete Pedagogical Academy in Graz and parish church at Oberwart are among the outstanding examples of brutalism in Austria, and their unbuildable Stadt Ragnitz megastructure resembled the projects of the Metabolists and Archigram. Domenig taught at Graz from 1980 and received the Grand Austrian State Prize for Architecture in 2004.

His first internationally acclaimed building was the Zentralsparkasse Branch, Favoritenstrasse in Vienna (1979), the "Z-bank". He worked on his own concrete house at Lake Ossiach, the Steinhaus (2008), from 1980 until 2008. In 1998 he won the international competition for the Documentation Center Nazi Party Rally Grounds in Nuremberg (2001), in the unfinished Congress Hall: a diagonal passage of glass and steel spears through the building's north head, a pun on and rebuttal of the Nazi architect Albert Speer, whose surname means "spear". Domenig, the son of a Nazi judge, was also confronting his own history.

facts.claim: Günther Domenig, 6 July 1934 – 15 June 2012; born in Klagenfurt; Graz University of Technology 1953–1959; practice with Eilfried Huth 1963–1973; exposed concrete, among the outstanding examples of brutalism in Austria (Pedagogical Academy Graz, Oberwart parish church); Stadt Ragnitz megastructure like the Metabolists and Archigram; pop-art temporary buildings for the 1972 Munich Olympics; Z-bank in Vienna his first internationally acclaimed work, expressionistic, counter-modernist; Steinhaus at Lake Ossiach; professor at Graz from 1980; works list: Zentralsparkasse bank, Vienna 1974–79; Steinhaus 1980–2008; Documentation Center 1998–2001; 1981 Austrian builders prize for the Z-branch Favoriten; 2004 Grand Austrian State Prize

name: Hans Poelzig
bio:
Hans Poelzig (1869–1936) was a German architect, painter and set designer whose work moved through Expressionism and the New Objectivity. Born in Berlin, he designed many industrial buildings after his training and in 1903 became director of the Breslau Academy of Art and Design, in today's Wrocław. He was made city architect of Dresden in 1916 and taught at the Technische Hochschule Berlin from 1920 to 1935, where Egon Eiermann was among his master students. He remodelled the Grosses Schauspielhaus in Berlin for Max Reinhardt in 1919 and designed the sets for the 1920 film The Golem.

The Four Domes Pavilion in Wrocław (1913) is now part of the Centennial Hall World Heritage Site. The Haus des Rundfunks in Berlin (1931) is the world's oldest self-contained broadcasting centre: he put three large studios at its centre, shielded from street noise by office wings around them. His best-known building, the IG Farben Building in Frankfurt (1930), has a 250-metre, gently curved main block with six wings; it was the largest building of the Weimar Republic, served as Eisenhower's headquarters from 1945, and now belongs to Goethe University.

name: Heatherwick Studio
bio:
Heatherwick Studio is a London design practice founded in 1994 by the English designer Thomas Heatherwick (born 1970), after he graduated from the Royal College of Art. The studio's work runs from objects to buildings: the UK pavilion at Expo 2010 in Shanghai, nicknamed the "Seed Cathedral", the cauldron for the 2012 Olympics in London, the New Routemaster bus, Vessel in New York and the Little Island pier on the Hudson.

Zeitz MOCAA in Cape Town (2017) turns a 57-metre grain silo of 1921–24 into a museum of contemporary art from Africa and its diaspora: galleries and a central atrium were cut out of its 42 concrete tubes, and glass caps on the shafts bring light down into a cathedral-like interior. The Hive, Nanyang Technological University (2015), in Singapore, replaces corridors and rectangular rooms with twelve tapering towers of rounded tutorial rooms around a central atrium, to bring students and staff together across subjects. 1000 Trees in Shanghai (2021), whose first phase opened that year, shapes offices, shops and galleries into two planted, mountain-like peaks that slope down to a park along Suzhou Creek.

name: Hector Guimard
bio:
Hector Guimard (1867–1942) was a French architect and designer prominent for his Art Nouveau work. Born in Lyon, he was a disciple of Viollet-le-Duc. Meeting Victor Horta in Brussels in 1895, where he saw the curving plant-like lines of the Hôtel Tassel, changed his style. Between 1890 and 1930 he built some 50 buildings, but Art Nouveau fell out of fashion in the 1910s, and by the 1960s most of his work had been demolished; his reputation revived in that decade. His wife was Jewish, and fearing war they settled in New York in 1938, where he died.

Castel Béranger (1898) was the first Art Nouveau apartment building in Paris and was chosen in the city's façade competition as one of the best new façades. Between 1900 and 1913 he designed the first generation of the Paris Metro Entrances (1900), 141 in all, in cast iron and glass painted green to look like weathered brass. The Hôtel Guimard (1912) on the Avenue Mozart was built from 1909 as his home and studio, with a studio for his wife, the painter Adeline Oppenheim Guimard.

name: Helmut Jahn
bio:
Helmut Jahn (1940–2021) was a German-American architect based in Chicago, known for The Center Potsdamer Platz in Berlin, the Messeturm in Frankfurt, the James R. Thompson Center in Chicago and Suvarnabhumi Airport in Bangkok. Born near Nuremberg, he studied in Munich and at the Illinois Institute of Technology. He joined C. F. Murphy Associates in 1967 and took sole control in 1981 as Murphy/Jahn. Inspired by Mies van der Rohe but opposed to the doctrinaire modernism of his followers, he joined the Chicago Seven in 1978; the Thompson Center (1985) earned him the nickname "Flash Gordon". He was killed in 2021 when two cars hit him as he cycled near his home.

11 Diagonal Street in Johannesburg (1983), a 22-floor office tower known as the diamond building, is shaped to reflect different views of the city from each angle. The Messeturm in Frankfurt (1991) is a 63-storey, 257-metre postmodern tower that rises into a cylinder and ends in a pyramid; it was Europe's tallest building until 1997. The Sony Center in Berlin (2000) has a public forum under an umbrella-like roof of steel, glass and fabric.

name: Hendrik Petrus Berlage
bio:
Hendrik Petrus Berlage (1856–1934) was a Dutch architect and designer, considered the father of modern architecture in the Netherlands and one of the fathers of the Amsterdam School. Born in Amsterdam, he studied at the Zurich Institute of Technology from 1875 to 1878. He drew on the brick architecture of Henry Hobson Richardson and the ideas of Viollet-le-Duc, and his load-bearing bare brick walls, with walls as the makers of form, became founding principles of the Dutch "Hollandse Zakelijkheid". He inspired most Dutch architectural groups of the 1920s, from the Amsterdam School to De Stijl, and received the RIBA Royal Gold Medal in 1932.

The Beurs van Berlage in Amsterdam (1903), an exchange, is red brick with an iron and glass roof; to Berlage its great brick walls stood for a democratic society: "as individuals insignificant, as a mass a power." For Anton and Helene Kröller-Müller he designed the Jachthuis Sint Hubertus (1920), a hunting lodge on their estate, now De Hoge Veluwe National Park. The Kunstmuseum Den Haag (Gemeentemuseum) (1935), built from 1931 in yellow brick, was finished by his son-in-law Emil Strasser after Berlage died.

name: Herbert Baker
bio:
Sir Herbert Baker (1862–1946) was an English architect, remembered as the dominant force in South African architecture, with a Neo-Classical style that projected imperial strength and permanence. Born in Kent, he trained with his cousin Arthur Baker and at the Royal Academy Schools, where Edwin Lutyens was a classmate. In 1891 he went to South Africa, where Cecil Rhodes asked him to rebuild his house, Groote Schuur. In 1925 he was brought in to plan Nairobi, a plan controversial for laying out racial segregation. His last work, the rebuilding of Sir John Soane's Bank of England behind its outer walls, has weighed on his reputation ever since.

The Pretoria Railway Station (1910) came in the same years as the Union Buildings in Pretoria (1913) for the new Union of South Africa: a 285-metre range of light sandstone with two wings and twin domed towers standing for English and Afrikaans around a semicircular court. In New Delhi he designed the Secretariat and, with Lutyens, Sansad Bhavan (Old Parliament House) (1927). The old friends fell out bitterly when Baker's Secretariat blocked the view of the Viceroy's House.

name: Hermann Henselmann
bio:
Hermann Henselmann (1905–1995) was a German architect best known for his buildings in East Germany in the 1950s and 1960s. Born in Roßla, he studied at the Kunstgewerbeschule in Berlin; his early houses were modernist, with a clear Bauhaus influence, and because of this and his partly Jewish ancestry the Nazi government barred him from private practice. After the war he stayed in East Berlin, persuaded by his friend Bertolt Brecht. He turned to Socialist Realism, designing the towers at each end of the Stalinallee, now Karl-Marx-Allee, then returned to modernism after Stalin's death. He was chief architect of Berlin from 1953 and retired in 1972.

The Hochhaus an der Weberwiese in Berlin (1952), a block of flats, was the first example of socialist classicism in East Germany. Plans for a "Signal Tower" that he drafted in 1958 became early designs for the Fernsehturm Berlin (1969), 368 metres high with its antenna and the tallest structure in Germany. The City-Hochhaus Leipzig (1972), built for the University of Leipzig in the shape of an open book, is at 142.5 metres the city's tallest multistorey building.

name: HOK
bio:
HOK is an American design, architecture, engineering and planning firm, founded in St. Louis in 1955 as Hellmuth, Obata + Kassabaum by George F. Hellmuth, Gyo Obata and George Kassabaum. In 1975 it was named architect of King Saud University in Riyadh, then the single largest building project in the world. Its sports arm, formed in 1983, became the separate firm Populous in 2009. HOK now has 28 offices across North America, Europe and Asia.

King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh (1983), opened by King Fahd that November, has four passenger terminals and, as the dominant building of the complex, a mosque for 5,000 worshippers inside and 4,000 more on its plaza. For the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) campus (2009) at Thuwal, HOK drew the master plan, with wind towers and solar panels; it was Saudi Arabia's first LEED-certified project and is the world's largest LEED Platinum campus. The Flame Towers in Baku (2012), three skyscrapers up to 182 metres high, are shaped as flames after Azerbaijan's name, "the Land of Fire", where natural gas flares from the ground.

name: Houshang Seyhoun
bio:
Houshang Seyhoun (1920–2014) was an Iranian architect, sculptor, painter and teacher who became famous in the 1950s for tombs of Iran's poets and scholars. He studied architecture at the University of Tehran under André Godard and Maxime Siroux, then at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris, where he finished in 1948 with a design for Avicenna's mausoleum at Hamadan. As dean of the University of Tehran's College of Fine Arts from 1961 he added Iran's historic architecture to the teaching. He believed that a good architect must, like a poet, be simple. After the Iranian Revolution he lived in exile in Vancouver.

Built after his competition win, the Avicenna Mausoleum in Hamadan (1954) rises as a spindle-shaped tower 28 metres high, inspired by the Ziyarid-era Kavus Tower. The Tomb of Nader Shah in Mashhad (1959) holds the grave of the ruler. The Omar Khayyam Mausoleum in Nishapur (1963), a white marble monument over the poet's grave, draws on Khayyam's work as poet, mathematician and astronomer, and a path from the garden lets blossoms fall on the tomb each spring, as Khayyam had wished.

name: Jean Prouvé
bio:
Jean Prouvé (1901–1984) was a French metalworker, self-taught architect and designer whose main achievement was carrying manufacturing technology from industry into architecture without losing its beauty; Le Corbusier called him a constructeur, joining architecture and engineering. Born in Nancy, he trained with blacksmiths and opened his first workshop in 1923, making wrought iron and then furniture and fittings of folded sheet metal. From the 1930s his workshops patented folded-metal building parts and prefabricated houses, among them the aluminium Maison Tropicale for Africa, and from 1947 his factory at Maxéville researched aluminium building. In 1971 he chaired the jury that chose Richard Rogers and Renzo Piano's design for the Centre Pompidou.

The Maison du Peuple, Clichy (1939), with the architects Eugène Beaudouin and Marcel Lods and the engineer Vladimir Bodiansky, is a historic monument. For MuMa (Musée d'art moderne André Malraux) in Le Havre (1961), designed by Atelier LWD, he made the aluminium louvres above the roof that control the light flooding in. The Accor Arena (Palais omnisports de Paris-Bercy) (1984), designed with Andrault-Parat and Aydin Guvan, is a pyramid whose sloping walls are covered in lawn.

name: John Andrews
bio:
John Andrews (1933–2022) was an Australian architect, described as Australia's first internationally recognised architect, with acclaimed buildings in Australia, Canada and the United States. Born in Sydney, he graduated from the University of Sydney in 1956 and studied at Harvard under Sigfried Giedion and José Luis Sert. He worked for John B. Parkin Associates near Toronto, taught at the University of Toronto from 1962 to 1970 and founded John Andrews Architects in Toronto in 1962, expanding to Sydney in 1973. He received the RAIA Gold Medal in 1980.

Scarborough College (Andrews Building) in Toronto (1964), the oldest building on the University of Toronto's Scarborough campus, is a megalithic brutalist structure of exposed concrete; its two wings meet at a central atrium, the Meeting Place, under a coffered concrete skylight. His office was part of the team for the CN Tower (1976), the 553-metre Toronto communications tower that was the world's tallest free-standing structure from 1975 to 2007. The Cameron Offices in Canberra (1976), government offices in a brutalist structuralist style built from 1970, were partly demolished in 2007–08.

name: John Lautner
bio:
John Lautner (1911–1994) was an American architect who worked mainly in California, mostly on houses, and is best remembered for his part in the Googie style and for several Atomic Age houses of the late 1950s and early 1960s. Born in Marquette, Michigan, he joined Frank Lloyd Wright's Taliesin Fellowship in 1933. He opened his own practice in 1938; his commissions of 1949–50 included Googie's Coffee House. The Elrod House (1968), perhaps his most widely seen work, became famous as a location in the James Bond film Diamonds Are Forever.

The Pearlman Mountain Cabin at Idyllwild (1957) is built as a cylinder on a circular platform over a large boulder among pines, its flat, overhanging roof carried on tree trunks set around it. The Chemosphere (Malin Residence) in Los Angeles (1960), a one-storey octagon reached by a funicular, stands on a concrete column nearly 30 feet high; Encyclopædia Britannica once called it "the most modern home built in the world". The Sheats-Goldstein Residence in Los Angeles (1963), designed from 1961, takes its cave-like form from the sandstone ledge it is built on.

name: Josef Paul Kleihues
bio:
Josef Paul Kleihues (1933–2004) was a German architect best known for decades of work on the "critical reconstruction" of Berlin; his approach has been called "poetic rationalist". Born in Rheine, he studied in Stuttgart and Berlin and founded his own practice in 1962. His Block 270 in Berlin-Wedding (1971) revived the traditional Berlin city block, and as director of the International Building Exhibition Berlin (IBA) from 1979 to 1987 he promoted critical reconstruction. Museums, from the Sprengel Museum in Hanover to the Museum of Prehistory in Frankfurt, brought him international recognition, and he chaired the jury that chose Daniel Libeskind for the Jewish Museum Berlin.

The Kant-Dreieck in Berlin (1994), an office building he won in a 1986 competition, carries on its roof a riveted sheet-metal sail that turns in the wind. He converted the Hamburger Bahnhof in Berlin (1996), a 19th-century railway terminus, into a museum of contemporary art. For the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago (1996) he was chosen after a 12-month search through more than 200 nominations; the five-storey building of Indiana limestone and hand-cast aluminium panels gave the museum seven times its former gallery space.

name: Joseph Allen Stein
bio:
Joseph Allen Stein (1912–2001) was an American architect who helped establish a regional modern architecture in the San Francisco Bay Area in the 1940s and 1950s, then spent most of his career in India. Born in Omaha, he worked for Richard Neutra before designing modest, low-cost houses in California. Investigated for his political views in the McCarthy years, he left the United States and in 1952 went to India to teach near Calcutta; in 1955 he planned the industrial town of Durgapur with Benjamin Polk. India awarded him the Padma Shri in 1992.

His buildings in New Delhi's Lodi Estate earned the area the nickname "Steinabad", and Joseph Stein Lane there is the only road in Delhi named after an architect. The India International Centre (1962), beside Lodhi Gardens, was voted the best building in Delhi in a 2008 Outlook magazine poll of architects. He also designed the Triveni Kala Sangam (1963), an arts centre with galleries and theatres. The India Habitat Centre (1993), for the housing agency HUDCO and nonprofit groups, turned an office brief into urban design: five blocks linked by aerial walkways around shared courtyards.

name: Kazuyo Sejima
bio:
Kazuyo Sejima (born 1956) is a Japanese architect who leads her own office, Kazuyo Sejima & Associates, and, with Ryue Nishizawa, the firm SANAA. Born in Mito, Ibaraki, she studied at Japan Women's University, finishing a master's degree in 1981, and worked for Toyo Ito until 1987, when she set up her own office; one of her first hires was Nishizawa, and in 1995 the two founded SANAA in Tokyo. In 2010 she and Nishizawa received the Pritzker Prize, making her the second woman to win it, and that year she became the first woman to direct the architecture section of the Venice Biennale.

The Gifu Kitagata Apartment (1998) in Gifu Prefecture is among her office's works of the 1990s. The New Museum in New York (2007), designed with Nishizawa as SANAA together with Gensler, opened on the Bowery in December 2007 as a seven-storey stack of white boxes, chosen because its flexibility suits the changing nature of contemporary art. The Sumida Hokusai Museum in Tokyo (2016), devoted to the ukiyo-e artist Katsushika Hokusai, is made of five interlocking volumes clad in reflective aluminium panels.
